gaps_after_the_critic.area: Invariant 2: the author-minted refusal and the kind_of_source vocabulary (sworn.py _resolve lines 1189-1213; sworn_verify.js resolve lines ~816-828)
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: Not one proposed mutation touches the single rule the whole format rests on — a receipt the agent produced this turn is the agent swearing to itself. The two halves of the refusal (kind_of_source in SOURCE_KINDS_AUTHOR, and sha256 in manifest.authored_sha256), the closed-vocabulary refusal for an unknown kind, and the malformed-vs-unresolved split between receipt_author_minted and manifest_integrity are all unmutated. A verifier that silently drops half of this still passes every digest vector whose manifests are honest.

gaps_after_the_critic.area: Manifest normalisation and the digest domain (Manifest.__init__/core/from_dict/intact/digest_or_none; JS Manifest constructor, core(), intact(), digestOrNull())
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: manifest_digest is a top-level field of the digested core and manifest.intact() gates every rN span. Untouched: authored_sha256 lowercasing, the sort inside core(), the rung key emitted only under sworn/manifest/0.2, the spec fallback for an unknown spec string, and intact()'s 'no declared digest means intact' fallback. Only rung_unknown ordering was proposed. A JCS-domain slip here changes the digest of every manifest without changing a single span verdict.

gaps_after_the_critic.area: The three tree handles: MemoryTree, SnapshotTree, GitTree (sworn.py lines 796-1030)
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: Roughly 240 lines with zero proposed mutations, and SnapshotTree is the handle the conformance vectors replay path:/prereg: through (C10). The whole UNRESOLVED reason vocabulary lives here — no_commit, commit_absent, path_absent, not_a_blob, receipt_too_large, prereg_not_in_tree, git_unavailable — plus the blob-mode gate that makes a symlink or gitlink not_a_blob, the MAX_RECEIPT_BYTES cap, and the commit != snapshot_commit rule that stops a snapshot answering for a commit it was not taken at. The JS side answers no_repository, so nothing cross-checks this.

gaps_after_the_critic.area: Canonical text construction and the offsets it hands every span (scan's cut/boundary block, both sides)
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: canonical_sha256 is in the digested core and start/end appear on every span verdict, yet the cut list, its sort, the boundaries map and the piece assembly are unmutated. This region also happens to be self-correcting in ways a study should measure deliberately (see the control below) — nobody established which parts are load-bearing and which are redundant.

gaps_after_the_critic.area: The sidecar layer: to_sidecar, render, load_sidecar (sworn.py lines 543-668)
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: This is the capsule discipline — the asserted round trip that refuses to emit a sidecar it cannot reproduce, the reversed event application that makes </sworn><sworn …> adjacency byte-exact, and load_sidecar's strict validation (exact key set, span ordering and non-overlap, empty-span refusal, UTF-8 boundary check, text-hashes-to-document.sha256). Every one of those refusals is a place where a malicious sidecar becomes a verified document, and none is mutated.

gaps_after_the_critic.area: verify()'s reconciliation of sidecar, commit and tree (sworn.py lines 1584-1625)
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: Three refusals and one assignment decide what evidence the verdict is even computed against: the sidecar-commit vs --commit disagreement, the embedded-vs-supplied manifest disagreement, the re-scan-reproduces-the-span-table check, and `tree.commit = commit`, which is the rule that a verdict is a function of the commit the document names and never of somebody's checkout. Unmutated.

gaps_after_the_critic.area: Receipt issuance and re-derivation: issue_receipt, _RECEIPT_OUTSIDE_DIGEST, _v0_shape, verify_receipt (sworn.py lines 1674-1755)
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: R9 — the digest covers the core WITHOUT coverage — is a one-tuple decision that nothing mutates, and verify_receipt's whole schema-aware branch (v0 digests its full body and is compared on a projected shape; v1 excludes coverage and reports coverage_reproduces advisory; same_verifier_build reported not hidden) is untested by the study. A receipt layer that stops distinguishing these still re-derives its own freshly minted receipts.

Ninety lines outside the digest, so the conformance vectors cannot see it at all — which makes it exactly where a mutation study earns its keep. The sworn-span masking, the recomputation of fenced regions on canonical (not inline) coordinates, the sentence splitter borrowed byte-for-byte from diffgate, the sentence_share floor and its 4-digit rounding, and the 0/0-is-null rule are all unmutated, and coverage_reproduces plus the CLI headline read every one of them.

gaps_after_the_critic.area: Detail fields that ride inside the digested core: occurrences counting, _safe_text truncation, digit_bearing_tokens, leaf_type naming
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: detail dicts are inside the core the digest covers, so a JS/Python divergence in a report-only number is a conformance failure. countBytes in JS carries a deliberate superseded-line construction to match Python's non-overlapping bytes.count, and nothing mutates it; _safe_text's 80-character limit and the '_Obj'/'NoneType'/'list' type names the two sides agree on by hand are likewise untouched.

gaps_after_the_critic.area: Python-side strict-JSON duplicate-key tracking and the CLI's report-never-gate contract
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: The JS dup-key mutation has no Python counterpart, so _json_strict's object_pairs_hook — the thing that makes pointer_ambiguous possible — is unmutated on the side that mints the receipts. Separately, the exit_codes decision (verify exits 0 for SWORN-FAILED, document-MALFORMED and UNSWORN alike; check exits 1 only when a receipt does not re-derive) is a stated invariant with no mutation behind it.

mutations.name: the short-needle bound moves by one byte
mutations.why: A needle of exactly 16 bytes over a whole receipt is currently accepted and goes on to HELD or FAILED needle_missing; mutated it becomes MALFORMED short_needle. The reported minimum_bytes detail is unchanged, so ONLY a 16-byte needle diverges — everything shorter and everything longer behaves identically. This is the classic careless one-sided edit (`<` vs `<=` on a documented minimum) and it is invisible unless the grammar emits a needle sitting exactly on the boundary.

mutations.name: the line-slice exemption from the short-needle refusal is dropped
mutations.old: if res["slice"] is None and len(needle) < SHORT_NEEDLE_BYTES:
mutations.why: v0.2 R3 exempts a line-slice haystack from the short-needle minimum because the author narrowed the haystack by naming it. Dropping the `res["slice"] is None` guard makes a short needle over a line slice MALFORMED short_needle in Python while JS still resolves it to HELD/FAILED. Requires a quote receipt carrying an #L line fragment AND a needle under 16 bytes — a two-feature conjunction the grammar may never draw together, which is exactly the kind of hole worth measuring.

mutations.name: needle counting stops rejecting two or more code spans
mutations.why: needleIn is the single needle extractor for quote, absent, and the pre-resolve bytes-only form check. Today two backtick code spans in one sworn span are MALFORMED needle_count; mutated, the first span is silently taken as the needle and the verdict becomes HELD or FAILED. Zero spans still returns needle_count so spans[0] is never indexed out of range and the file runs. Reachable whenever the grammar puts two inline code spans in a quote or absent span.

mutations.name: the hash-over-partial refusal is dropped by a copy-paste of the absent check
mutations.why: The two partial refusals sit on adjacent lines; duplicating the first kind onto the second is the exact careless edit this study is looking for. The body still returns hash_over_partial but is now unreachable (absent was already caught one line above), so a hash sworn over a partial receipt is no longer refused and instead resolves and compares a sha256 against a fragment. Python still returns MALFORMED hash_over_partial. Only reachable if the grammar mints a hash declaration whose receipt carries a fragment.

mutations.name: the absent-over-partial pre-resolve refusal is disabled
mutations.why: "exec" is in RESERVED_KINDS and is returned as kind_reserved several lines earlier, so this branch becomes dead code — a clean single-effect removal of one refusal with no second symptom. An absent declaration over a partial receipt now falls through to _resolve instead of being refused up front. The interesting question is whether the harness sees it at all: the post-resolve completeness check may still catch it as MALFORMED absent_over_partial, differing only in detail ({"complete": False} instead of {"receipt": ...}), or resolve may return UNRESOLVED first and mask the change entirely.

mutations.name: the hash digest loses its lowercase normalisation
mutations.why: res.sha256 is always lowercase hex, so dropping the case fold turns every correct uppercase or mixed-case digest from HELD into FAILED digest_mismatch, and also changes the `stated` string in the detail. This is a removed normalisation step, the highest-yield mutation class for differential testing, but it is only visible if the grammar ever emits a digest containing an uppercase hex letter — the HEXRUN regex accepts A-F, so the question is whether the generator ever produces one.

mutations.name: 96-character hex runs stop counting as competing digests
mutations.why: A hash span containing one 64-hex run plus a 96-hex run (a SHA-384) is currently MALFORMED digest_form on both sides, because a second digest-shaped run makes the binding ambiguous. Dropping 96 lets Python proceed to compare the 64-run while JS still refuses. The constant feeds both _check_hash and the pre-resolve form check in _adjudicate, so the change is internally consistent and the file runs. I suspect the grammar does not emit 96-character hex runs at all — this is deliberately a hole probe rather than a likely catch.

mutations.name: the numeric token stops stripping a trailing colon
mutations.why: _TOKEN pulls the colon into the token, so a span reading `precision 0.55:` yields the token "0.55:" which _GRAM.fullmatch rejects. Mutated, Python returns MALFORMED number_grammar where JS strips the colon and returns HELD or FAILED value_mismatch. A removed normalisation step on the numeric kind, reachable whenever the grammar writes a number immediately before a colon.

mutations.name: absent misses a needle sitting at byte offset zero
mutations.why: The find result 0 means found at the very start of the receipt. With `> 0` that case reports HELD — a false negative on the one kind whose whole purpose is swearing something is not there, and the worst possible direction for the error. Python's `needle in hay` is position-independent and still returns FAILED needle_present. Only reachable if the grammar ever places the needle bytes at offset 0 of a complete receipt, which is why it is a good test of whether the generator explores span positions or only span content.

mutations.name: the absent haystack local is renamed consistently
mutations.why: CONTROL: a local variable renamed at every one of its three uses inside _check_absent. The dict keys, the verdict, the reason and the detail values are byte-identical for every input, so the verdict-core digest cannot change. If the harness flags this it is detecting that the file was edited, not that the two implementations diverged, and every catch it reports on the other nine mutations has to be discounted accordingly.

mutations.name: SWORN-HELD stops caring about MALFORMED spans
mutations.why: A document whose only bad spans are MALFORMED now reports SWORN-HELD instead of SWORN-FAILED. This is exactly the decision the spec calls out ('sworn_total_counts_malformed'), and it is the single most plausible careless edit: someone reads 'held means nothing failed' and drops the second conjunct. The random grammar almost certainly produces MALFORMED-only documents (empty spans, bad kinds, digest_form), so the harness should see this.

mutations.name: the top-level unresolved count folds in MALFORMED
mutations.why: `unresolved` is a redundant projection of counts, so a careless edit could 'helpfully' widen it to mean 'everything that did not adjudicate'. It changes the core on any document with a MALFORMED span while leaving counts and document_verdict identical — a test that only diffs verdicts and counts would miss it.

mutations.name: spans with no provenance land in a differently named rung bucket
mutations.why: The rungs histogram key for every span that never resolved. A one-sided rename of this bucket label is the kind of thing that happens when one implementation is 'tidied'. Reached by any document with an UNRESOLVED or MALFORMED span, which should be most of them — if the harness misses this, its digest is not covering the rungs block at all.

mutations.name: an undeclared rung is treated as an unknown rung
mutations.why: The trust ladder distinguishes three states: ok, undeclared (manifest/0.1, or 0.2 with no rung — resolves at rung `undeclared`) and unknown (L3 or a string nobody defined — UNRESOLVED). Collapsing undeclared into unknown turns every rn span under a rung-less manifest from HELD/FAILED into UNRESOLVED rung_unknown. Reached only if the grammar emits manifests without a rung; if it always sets one, this mutation survives and that is a hole in the ladder's coverage.

mutations.name: comment reworded above the bytes-only form checks
mutations.new: // form checks that need only the span bytes run first, before any receipt is opened
mutations.old: // bytes-only form checks run BEFORE any receipt is opened
mutations.why: Semantics-preserving control. If the harness reports a divergence here it is detecting that a file changed, not that behaviour diverged.

mutations.name: UNSWORN outranks a malformed document
mutations.why: Pure branch reorder. The spec's 'document_malformed_is_failed' decision says unbalanced fences or undecodable UTF-8 yield SWORN-FAILED and never UNSWORN; swapping the two branches makes a document that is malformed AND carries zero declarations report UNSWORN. Reachable only when the grammar produces an unbalanced-fence or invalid-UTF-8 document with no sworn spans in it — a corner the generator may or may not hit.

mutations.name: sworn_total stops counting the WITHHELD verdict
mutations.new: sworn_total = sum(counts[v] for v in VERDICTS if v != "WITHHELD")
mutations.why: WITHHELD is declared in VERDICTS but no code path in either implementation ever emits it, so dropping it from the total is invisible to any input the grammar can build. Deliberately aimed at that dead verdict: if the harness cannot see this, the finding is that the fifth verdict is uncovered on both sides, and sworn_total's definition over it is untested.

mutations.name: the committed-provenance rung bucket is renamed
mutations.why: path:/prereg: receipts only acquire provenance when a repository tree is supplied; the JS implementation has none (SPEC B1 returns no_repository), so a harness that digests both sides must run Python with tree=None too. That makes this branch dead in the differential, and renaming its key should sail through — a hole covering the entire committed-provenance half of the rungs histogram.

mutations.name: unresolved receipts are reported as WITHHELD
mutations.why: Relabels every resolution failure (manifest_absent, no_repository, manifest_id_missing, rung_unknown) with the otherwise-unused fifth verdict. It moves counts between two buckets, changes the top-level `unresolved` field, and leaves sworn_total and document_verdict untouched — so a harness that keys on document_verdict alone would not notice. Very reachable: no_repository alone should fire on every path:/prereg: span.

mutations.name: comment reworded above the rungs histogram
mutations.new: # manifest declared; it is counted so a reader sees it as prominently as the verdict itself.
mutations.old: # manifest declared, counted so a reader sees it at the same prominence as the verdict.
mutations.why: Semantics-preserving control on the Python side, adjacent to two real mutations in the same block. A guard that flags this is flagging edits, not divergence.

mutations.name: half-even becomes half-up in the JS BigInt rounder
mutations.why: The `>` to `>=` widening makes the tie case round away from zero unconditionally, so the second clause is dead and Dec.canon is ROUND_HALF_UP while the detail still advertises ROUND_HALF_EVEN. Any exact tie at the printed precision (0.25 to 1 frac digit, 1.5 to 0) flips lhs, which can flip HELD to FAILED. This is the classic one-sided edit: a maintainer 'simplifying' a rounding condition on one side only.

mutations.name: the scientific-notation threshold in Dec.toString moves by one decade
mutations.why: Python's to-scientific-string uses plain notation while leftdigits > -6; at leftdigits == -5 the JS side now switches to E-notation. `receipt` in the detail is leaf.toString(), so a receipt scalar like 1e-7 prints '0.0000001' on Python and '1E-7' on JS. Someone porting the CPython _decimal comment can easily transcribe the bound off by one, and nothing else in the file cross-checks it.

mutations.name: signed-zero folding only applies when fractional digits are printed
mutations.why: Python's _canon folds -0 to 0 unconditionally via q.copy_abs(). Gating on frac lets a negative value that rounds to zero at zero fractional digits print '-0' on JS and '0' on Python — so a span reading '-0' against a receipt of -0.4 flips HELD/FAILED. I doubt the grammar reaches it: it needs a negative leaf small enough to round to zero AND an integer printed token, which is a narrow corner. That is exactly why it is worth firing.

mutations.name: digit-bearing detection drops non-ASCII decimal digits
mutations.why: Python's `\d` on str is Unicode category Nd, so a token of Arabic-Indic or Devanagari digits counts as digit-bearing there and is then rejected by _GRAM as number_grammar. With ASCII-only JS the same token is invisible, so digit_bearing goes to length 0 and the reason becomes number_count instead — different reason, different digit_bearing_tokens detail. A grammar that only emits ASCII numerals will never see this, which makes it a good probe for whether the generator has any non-ASCII digit vocabulary at all.

mutations.name: reworded doc comment above Dec.toString
mutations.new: /** to-scientific-string, exactly as Python's str(Decimal) prints it. [B4 row 7] */
mutations.why: Control. Pure comment rewrite inside the decimal machinery, on the method most likely to be touched by the other mutations in this region. No token of executable code changes and no verdict, reason or detail can differ. If the harness reports a disagreement here it is detecting that the file was edited, not that the implementations diverged.

mutations.name: Python quantize rounds half-up instead of half-even
mutations.why: The mirror image of the JS rounder mutation, applied to the other side so the study can tell whether the harness's tie coverage is symmetric. decimal accepts the rounding mode as its literal string so the module still imports and _canon still runs; only ties move. The ROUNDING constant reported in `detail` is untouched, so the receipt keeps claiming ROUND_HALF_EVEN while the arithmetic no longer is.

mutations.name: the working precision in _canon is one digit short
mutations.why: The quantized result has adjusted+frac+1 significant digits, so dropping the +2 leaves the context one digit short and quantize raises InvalidOperation, which _check_numeric catches and converts to MALFORMED leaf_not_numeric. Confirmed at runtime with a 31-digit leaf. It only bites once adjusted+frac reaches the 28 floor, and the adjusted()>320 gate leaves a wide band above that where it does bite — but a grammar that emits human-sized numbers will never reach 28 significant digits, so I expect this one to survive and expose a magnitude hole.

mutations.name: the adjusted-exponent magnitude gate moves by one
mutations.why: Rejects a receipt scalar whose adjusted exponent is exactly 320 as MALFORMED leaf_not_numeric while JS still accepts it and proceeds to compare. Behaviour differs on a single exponent value, so it is only visible if the generator ever emits a number right at the 1e320 boundary. A bound like this is precisely what gets nudged in a one-sided edit, and precisely what a random grammar over plausible magnitudes never lands on.

mutations.name: fractional-digit count taken from the raw token, before normalisation
mutations.new: frac = len(tok.split(".", 1)[1]) if "." in tok else 0
mutations.old: frac = len(t.split(".", 1)[1]) if "." in t else 0
mutations.why: `t` is the token with commas removed, the Unicode minus folded, and the trailing percent stripped; `tok` still carries the percent. For '12.5%' the count becomes 2 instead of 1 (verified), so both sides quantize to a different scale: Python compares at two fractional digits while JS compares at one, changing `printed`, `receipt_rounded`, `fractional_digits` and the rounding boundary itself. Percent-suffixed numbers are ordinary prose, so the grammar plausibly reaches this — and reading the pre-normalised variable one line too early is a very natural slip.

mutations.name: reworded _canon docstring
mutations.new: """The single canonical decimal string both sides use: half-even quantized, zero unsigned."""
mutations.old: """One canonical decimal string for both sides: quantized half-even, signed zero folded."""
mutations.why: Control on the Python side, deliberately placed on the same function as two of the real mutations so it exercises the same file region. A docstring is not consulted by any verdict path, so no digest byte can move. Paired with the JS control it gives the study one semantics-preserving edit per implementation, which is what distinguishes a divergence detector from an edit detector.

mutations.name: fence indent cap moves from 3 spaces to 4
mutations.why: fencedRegions implements the spec-literal `^ {0,3}`{3,}`; with the bound at 4 a line indented by four spaces (which the spec says is indented code, NOT a fence) starts toggling fence state. The grammar's FENCES list contains both "   ```" and "    ```", so the 4-space case is generated; a careless port of the regex `{0,3}` into a hand-written space loop is exactly this off-by-one.

mutations.name: an inline code run closes on a LONGER backtick run
mutations.why: CommonMark closes a code span only on a backtick run of equal length; `>=` lets a longer run close it, so the skipped region (and therefore which `<sworn` tags are seen as live text) changes whenever a line mixes 1-, 2- and 3-backtick runs. The quote-sentence generator emits ticks of 1, 2 or 3 and fillers are often empty, so mixed runs on one line are reachable. Writing `>=` instead of `==` is the classic one-sided scanner slip.

mutations.name: a comment can no longer open exactly where the previous one closed
mutations.why: With `>` the `<!--` sitting immediately at the end of the previous comment is not recognised as a new comment, so a sworn tag inside that second comment never gets hidden_commitment and is adjudicated as an ordinary span. Needs two comment parts with an empty filler between them — the grammar can produce it, but rarely, so this probes whether 150k cases actually reach adjacent comments.

mutations.name: the span code-point cap becomes exclusive (300 now fails)
mutations.why: Only a span of exactly 300 code points changes verdict (HELD/FAILED -> MALFORMED length_cap). The grammar makes over-cap spans by repeating inner text 20-60 times, so it lands nowhere near the boundary — a hole I expect nobody catches. Boundary conditions on a cap are the single most common one-sided edit.

mutations.name: the tag-candidate lookahead stops excluding _ and -
mutations.why: `<sworn-note>` / `<sworn_note>` stop being narrative text and become tag-shaped candidates, i.e. MALFORMED tag_syntax declarations that flip the whole document to SWORN-FAILED. The grammar's only near-miss stem is `<swornx`, which stays excluded by [A-Za-z0-9] — so the mutation is invisible to it. This is the shape a hand-transcribed regex loses first.

mutations.name: a stray closer no longer counts as a lexical failure
mutations.why: Dropping stray_closer from lexicalBad makes lexical_ok true for a document containing a bare </sworn>, so canonical text is computed (and canonical_sha256 stops being null) where the Python side still refuses it. The grammar emits a bare </sworn> as its own part about 2% of the time, so this should be caught — it is the caught-side control for the classification list.

mutations.name: reword the fence comment (control)
mutations.new: // a fence delimiter line: 0-3 spaces of indent, then three or more backticks
mutations.why: Pure comment text; no token of the program changes. If the harness flags this, it is detecting edits rather than divergence.

mutations.name: hidden_commitment window includes the byte just past the comment
mutations.why: comment_end is the offset one past `-->`, so `<=` marks a tag that starts immediately AFTER a closed comment as a hidden commitment: MALFORMED instead of whatever it would have been. The grammar puts a comment part and a span part next to each other with an empty filler often enough that this should be reachable — an inclusive/exclusive slip on an end offset.

mutations.name: empty span inside a comment keeps the hidden_commitment reason
mutations.new: if not d["inner"] and d["malformed"] is None:
mutations.old: if not d["inner"] and d["malformed"] in (None, "hidden_commitment"):
mutations.why: The spec makes empty_span outrank hidden_commitment because a zero-length span cannot be represented in the sidecar. Dropping the second case leaves the reason string as hidden_commitment for a zero-byte span written inside an HTML comment; both are MALFORMED, so only the reason field in the verdict core diverges. Requires the conjunction (comment AND invalid kind giving empty inner), so it tests whether the grammar composes hazards or only visits them one at a time.

mutations.name: rename the code-span cursor q -> cursor (control)
mutations.why: A consistent local-variable rename inside the inline-code-span scanner: every read and write moves together, the loop is otherwise byte-identical, and the function has no other q. A larger, more code-like edit than a comment reword, so it is the stronger of the two controls — any guard that fires here is reacting to churn, not to behaviour.

mutations.name: path: receipts no longer refuse a leading ':' (git pathspec magic)
mutations.why: Drops one of three grammar guards on a path: target. `path::a.json` currently parses to MALFORMED receipt_form on both sides; mutated, JS accepts it and falls through to UNRESOLVED no_repository while Python still refuses. The generator mints `path::a.json` explicitly, so this is squarely reachable. A careless one-sided edit does exactly this: someone tightening the check in Python and 'simplifying' the JS chain to match.

mutations.name: JSON Pointer unescaping applies ~0 before ~1 (RFC 6901 order reversed)
mutations.why: The classic RFC 6901 ordering bug: with ~1 first, the token `~01` decodes to the literal `~1`; with ~0 first it decodes to `/`. Every other input decodes identically, so only a fragment containing `~01` (or `~00`) can see it. The grammar's receipt pool carries `r1#/~0` and `r1#/~2` and nothing else with a tilde, so I expect this MISSED — a real hole in the escaping rule the spec names explicitly.

mutations.name: a line span with equal endpoints (#L5-L5) is refused as receipt_form
mutations.why: Turns the descending-range refusal into a refusal of degenerate-but-legal ranges too. `#L3-L3` must parse as the single line 3; mutated JS calls it malformed. The grammar only ever emits L1, L1-L3, L9 and L0 — no equal-endpoint range and no descending range — so neither the original guard nor this off-by-one is exercised. Expect MISSED, and note the descending case is untested for the same reason.

mutations.name: line slice includes the last selected line's terminating LF
mutations.why: The documented rule excludes the final selected line's LF. Adding 1 keeps it, so every #L1 / #L1-L3 slice over a payload whose last selected line ends in \n grows by one byte. haystack_bytes rides in the quote detail and therefore in the digest, so this should be CAUGHT — `r1#L1` and `r1#L1-L3` are minted often and kind=quote is a sixth of the kind pool.

mutations.name: line slice starting past line 1 swallows the previous line's LF
mutations.why: The mirror image of the end-bound mutation, on the begin bound. It changes nothing when first === 1 and shifts the slice one byte left otherwise. The grammar's only line anchors are L1, L1-L3, L9 and L0: first is 1 whenever a slice resolves, and L9 is always past EOF, so the `positions[first - 2] + 1` branch never yields a value in 150000 cases. Expect MISSED — half of lineSlice is dead under this generator.

mutations.name: rung_unknown now yields to manifest_id_missing when the id is absent
mutations.why: Reorders two refusals in the rN manifest lookup: a manifest declaring an uncheckable rung (L3, L0, l1, 7) that also lacks the named receipt now reports manifest_id_missing instead of rung_unknown. Both conditions co-occur often — a third of the rung pool is bad and the receipt pool mints r3 and r10, which a manifest holding only r1..r4 usually lacks — so expect CAUGHT. Reordering guards is exactly the edit a refactor makes on one side only.

mutations.name: path: targets may contain '..' segments
mutations.new: if any(seg in ("", ".") for seg in target.split("/")):
mutations.old: if any(seg in ("", ".", "..") for seg in target.split("/")):
mutations.why: Removes the traversal refusal from the Python grammar only. `path:../a.json` and `path:a/../b.json` are both in the generator's receipt pool and both currently land on MALFORMED receipt_form; mutated, Python parses them and returns UNRESOLVED no_repository while JS still refuses. Expect CAUGHT — and it is the exact shape of a security-relevant one-sided regression.

mutations.name: prereg: digests are no longer case-folded
mutations.why: Drops the normalisation that makes `prereg:AB..` and `prereg:ab..` name the same object. The grammar accepts mixed case (the fullmatch is [0-9a-fA-F]{64}) but only ever mints `prereg:` + 'a'*64, and verify() is never handed a tree, so a prereg receipt short-circuits to UNRESOLVED no_repository before target is ever used. Expect MISSED: the whole prereg resolution path, normalisation included, is unreachable from this harness.

mutations.name: array index bound in pointer walking is off by one
mutations.new: if not re.fullmatch(r"0|[1-9][0-9]*", t) or int(t) > len(obj):
mutations.old: if not re.fullmatch(r"0|[1-9][0-9]*", t) or int(t) >= len(obj):
mutations.why: Lets a pointer address index == len(obj), which should be pointer_unresolvable but instead indexes off the end and raises IndexError out of _resolve. Loud on any input that reaches it — and nothing does: every manifest payload is a top-level object, and the only pointer that touches a list is `r1#/a/b`, which stops ON the list rather than walking into it. The list branch of _walk_pointer is never entered. Expect MISSED.

mutations.name: control: reword the _walk_pointer docstring
mutations.new: """Returns (value, 'ok') or (None, reason). A key duplicated ON the path is ambiguous."""
mutations.old: """Returns (value, 'ok') or (None, reason). A duplicated key ON the path is ambiguous."""
mutations.why: Semantics-preserving: a docstring reword inside the pointer walker, the hottest function in this region. If the differential harness flags this, it is detecting that a file changed rather than that the two implementations diverged, and every other result in the region becomes uninterpretable.

mutations.name: the UTF-8 validator stops rejecting encoded surrogates
mutations.old: if (cp < min || cp > 0x10ffff || (cp >= 0xd800 && cp <= 0xdfff)) return i;
mutations.why: firstInvalidUtf8 reproduces Python's UnicodeDecodeError.start, and that offset lands in document_malformed.at, which is inside the digested core. Dropping the surrogate clause makes CESU-8 bytes (ED A0 80) decode-clean on the JS side, so the reported `at` moves to a later byte or falls through to the terminal `return 0`. The generator only ever appends b"\xff\xfe", which trips the `else return i` arm on the very first test, so every interior branch of this hand-rolled validator is dead weight the harness cannot see. A careless one-sided edit does exactly this: the surrogate clause looks redundant next to the 0x10ffff bound.

mutations.name: the three-byte overlong bound drops from U+0800 to U+0080
mutations.new: else if (b >= 0xe0 && b <= 0xef) { need = 2; cp = b & 0x0f; min = 0x80; }
mutations.old: else if (b >= 0xe0 && b <= 0xef) { need = 2; cp = b & 0x0f; min = 0x800; }
mutations.why: `min` is the overlong floor for a three-byte sequence. At 0x80 the classic overlong encodings E0 9F BF (U+07FF written in three bytes) sail through, so when a document carries both an overlong sequence and a later hard-invalid byte, JS reports the later offset while Python's decoder refuses at the overlong one. Same mechanism as above: document_malformed.at is digested, but the grammar never emits an overlong sequence, so the whole overlong-refusal machinery is untested. The two hex constants 0x800 and 0x80 differ by one character, which is precisely the kind of slip a one-sided edit makes.

mutations.name: the JSON reader stops refusing a BOM
mutations.new: if (text.length && text.charCodeAt(0) === 0xfffe) throw new Error("BOM-prefixed JSON");
mutations.old: if (text.length && text.charCodeAt(0) === 0xfeff) throw new Error("BOM-prefixed JSON");
mutations.why: Python's _json_strict refuses a leading U+FEFF outright; this line is the JS mirror. Swapping the sentinel to 0xfffe (the byte-swapped BOM, which never appears as a decoded character) removes the refusal entirely while keeping the line looking correct. I expect this to survive: jsonStrict is only reached through jsonStrictBytes on receipt payload bytes, and every payload in the grammar is bare ASCII JSON, while the manifest arrives via jsonPlain(JSON.stringify(...)). The harness does inject a BOM into 1% of documents (39 of 4000 sampled) - but a document is not JSON, so those BOMs are inert filler bytes and never reach this check. That gap is the finding: the harness looks like it covers BOMs and does not.

mutations.name: the lone-surrogate refusal on a pointer leaf is neutered
mutations.why: Python raises UnicodeEncodeError when it tries to .encode("utf-8") a leaf holding a lone surrogate and returns MALFORMED/leaf_not_string; this regex is the JS stand-in for that raise. Testing the empty string instead makes the branch permanently false, so a quote against a leaf like "\ud800" would compare surrogate-bearing text as if it were encodable. The manifest payloads in the grammar are fixed byte literals with no \u escapes anywhere, so no leaf can ever hold a surrogate and this whole refusal is unreachable - a hole exactly where the two languages disagree most sharply about what a string is.

mutations.name: the opener's end offset is measured in UTF-16 units, not bytes
mutations.why: This is the bytes-to-text seam of the whole scanner: OPENER_RE matches over a decoded window, and utf8() converts the match length back into a byte advance so it lines up with Python's om.end() on bytes. Using the JS string length instead makes openerEnd short whenever the opener contains any non-ASCII, which shifts d.inner, every span's start/end, and the canonical bytes. The receipt attribute allows any character except <>, CR and LF, but every entry in the generator's RECEIPTS and KINDS tables is pure ASCII, so byte length and UTF-16 length coincide on all 150000 cases. I expect this to survive, and it is the most consequential hole in the region.

mutations.name: a line-range slice keeps its terminating LF
mutations.why:
The spec says the last selected line's terminating LF is excluded; Python's _line_slice uses positions[last-1] as an exclusive end. Adding one appends the LF to every #Ln slice that is not at EOF. The slice becomes the quote haystack, so haystack_bytes in the verdict detail shifts by one and the digest diverges. This one should be CAUGHT: r1#L1 and r1#L1-L3 carry real weight in RECEIPTS and the multi-line payload b'line one
line two
line three
' is in the pool. It is the reachable control point against which the CR/LF holes are measured.

mutations.name: the strict-decode comment is reworded
mutations.new: /** Strict decode: null when the bytes do not decode as UTF-8 (document-level MALFORMED). */
mutations.old: /** Strict decode: returns null when the bytes are not UTF-8 (the document-level MALFORMED). */
mutations.why: CONTROL. A pure comment reword on the central decode helper - no token of executable code changes, and the mutant produces byte-identical digests. If the harness flags this it is detecting edits, not divergence, and every other result in this region is void.

mutations.name: the invalid-UTF-8 offset reports the end of the bad sequence
mutations.why: UnicodeDecodeError carries both .start and .end; the spec pins .start, and the JS side reimplements exactly that in firstInvalidUtf8. Reporting .end shifts the digested document_malformed.at by one for the trailing b'\xff\xfe' hazard and by more for a truncated multi-byte tail. This should be CAUGHT: I measured 41 invalid-UTF-8 documents in 4000 sampled cases (~1%, so roughly 1500 in the full run). start/end is the classic one-sided slip when someone re-reads the exception object.

mutations.name: the span length cap counts bytes instead of code points
mutations.why: SPAN_CAP_CODEPOINTS is a cap on characters, not bytes, and the detail dict already reports len(inner) separately as "bytes" - conflating the two is the obvious careless edit, and it silently makes the cap stricter for non-ASCII text. It changes both the threshold and the reported code_points value. This should be CAUGHT, but only just: I measured 257 over-cap spans in 4000 cases of which only 3 contained non-ASCII (the generator's ٣.٥ and −0.0154 tokens), so it rides on about 0.07% of cases. A useful calibration point for how thin the margin is between caught and missed here.

mutations.name: CR stops counting as span whitespace
mutations.why: This is the empty_span refusal - a span whose inner is only ASCII whitespace is MALFORMED. Dropping \r from the strip set means a CRLF-only inner is no longer empty and falls through to a kind-specific verdict instead. The harness looks like it covers this: FILLERS contains "\r\n" and "\r", and 1% of documents get every LF rewritten to CRLF. But I found 0 spans in 4000 cases whose inner is whitespace-only AND contains a CR - the CRs the generator produces always land between spans, never inside one. I expect this to SURVIVE, which is the sharpest kind of hole: a hazard the harness deliberately injects and still cannot route to the code that handles it.

mutations.name: comment reworded in the sha256 header (control)
mutations.new: 60 lines of FIPS 180-4 is the cheaper dependency to carry.
mutations.old: 60 lines of FIPS 180-4 is the cheaper dependency.
mutations.why: Pure prose edit inside a block comment; no token of executable code moves. Verified: file parses, all 1689-vector-shaped API surface unchanged. If the harness flags this, it is detecting that a file was edited, not that the two implementations diverged. CONTROL.

mutations.name: sha256 message padding reserves one byte too many
mutations.why: FIPS 180-4 needs len+1+8 bytes to fit; +9 spends an extra block exactly when ml % 64 == 55. Probed against node crypto over lengths 0..199: diverges at 55, 119, 183 and agrees on the other 197. Every case digests the whole document (document.inline_sha256), the canonical bytes, and the JCS core, so roughly 3-in-64 of them should trip. A careless one-sided 'fix' to the padding arithmetic looks exactly like this and is right 97% of the time.

mutations.name: sha256 drops the high word of the 64-bit length field
mutations.why: The high 32 bits of the bit-length only become non-zero at 2^29 bytes = 512 MiB. Probed: identical digests to node crypto on all 200 short lengths. The grammar composes documents of at most a few kilobytes, so this can never be reached — a genuine hole. Anyone simplifying the length encoding on a 32-bit-looking value would write exactly this and every test would stay green.

mutations.name: JCS drops key sorting for Map/JObj objects
mutations.why: This is the branch JCS takes for a parsed manifest: Manifest.core() builds a Map in insertion order (spec, harness, turn, minted_at, authored_sha256, receipts, rung) whose sorted order is completely different, and every receipt entry is a JObj too. Probed: {"spec":..,"harness":..} serialises as {"authored_sha256":[],"harness":"h",...} before and as {"spec":"s","harness":"h",...} after. Feeds core.manifest_digest, present in ~88% of cases. The sibling plain-object branch three lines below keeps its sort, so this is the half-repair a one-sided edit produces.

mutations.name:
JCS emits 
 instead of the short \n escape
mutations.why: Both forms are legal JSON but RFC 8785 pins the short escape, and Python's json.dumps emits \n, so the digests would part company on any core string containing a newline. Measured over 3000 grammar cases: the only control code points that ever reach a core string are U+0009 (4 times) and U+000D (13 times) - U+000A never once, because tag_syntax `raw` is truncated at the first newline and needle text is reported only as a byte count. So the \t and \r escapes beside it are reachable and this one is not. A precise hole, one line away from two mutations that would be caught.

mutations.name: JCS \u-escapes every non-ASCII code point
mutations.why: RFC 8785 requires non-ASCII to pass through raw; Python's json.dumps(ensure_ascii=False) does. Probed: jcsString('harness with é') becomes "harness with é". The grammar feeds 'harness with é' and 'a name with é.md' straight into the core - measured 4153 non-ASCII code points across 3000 cases - so this should be caught immediately. Worth noting the branch being widened is itself dead under this grammar: no core string in 3000 cases held a code point in 0x00-0x08 or 0x0e-0x1f, so only the added clause is live.

mutations.name: strict JSON parser stops remembering duplicate keys
mutations.why: Reads as a plausible set-hygiene edit and leaves `dups` permanently empty. Probed: jsonStrict('{"dup": 1, "dup": 2}') reports dups ['dup'] before and [] after. The grammar ships a {"dup": 1, "dup": 2} receipt payload and an r1#/dup pointer, so the JS side would resolve the last value where Python still returns pointer_ambiguous. Should be caught - this is the reachable half of the duplicate-key question, paired with the NaN mutation below which is the unreachable half.

mutations.name: JSON number lexer no longer accepts a leading minus
mutations.why: parseValue peels off -Infinity before falling through here, so dropping -? looks defensible; it is not, and every negative number becomes a parse failure for the whole receipt. Probed: jsonStrict('{"neg": -0.0}') throws 'Expecting value at 8' after the edit while '{"e": 1e5}' still parses. The grammar's {"neg": -0.0, "e": 1e5} payload makes this reachable, turning HELD/FAILED numeric spans into receipt_not_json on the JS side only.

mutations.name: strict JSON reads integers as int rather than Decimal
mutations.why: The one-line docstring promise is 'every number as a Decimal of its own digits (never a float)'; int satisfies 'never a float' and looks harmless. But _check_numeric guards with `not isinstance(leaf, Decimal)`, so every integer leaf becomes MALFORMED/leaf_not_numeric instead of being compared. Probed: the {"passed": 12} payload yields Decimal('12') before and int 12 after. The grammar pairs that payload with r1#/passed and kind numeric constantly, so this should be caught in the first handful of cases - it is the strongest reachable mutation on the Python side.

mutations.name: strict JSON reads NaN/Infinity as float rather than Decimal
mutations.why: Sits on the same line as the mutation above and is the obvious 'consistency' edit, but it is invisible: _json_strict only ever sees the ten fixed receipt payloads, none of which contains a NaN, Infinity or -Infinity literal, and the manifest never goes through this path (Python takes it as a dict, JS via JSON.stringify, which cannot emit those tokens). Probed: json.loads('{"z": NaN}') gives Decimal before and float after, which would flip leaf_not_numeric detail and the is_finite guard - if anything ever generated it. The declared 'NaN/Infinity kept as Decimal so one bad leaf cannot hide the rest of the file' behaviour is entirely untested by this harness.

mutations.name: the author-minted refusal drops the authored_sha256 half
mutations.old: if kos in SOURCE_KINDS_AUTHOR or sha in manifest.authored_sha256:
mutations.why: Invariant 2 has two halves: the kind the harness recorded, and set membership in the digests of every byte-object the agent produced this turn. This mutant keeps the first and drops the second, so a receipt the harness honestly labelled tool_stdout but whose bytes the agent itself wrote resolves and can HELD instead of MALFORMED receipt_author_minted. No mutation in the study touches this rule at all.

mutations.name: the JS manifest stops case-folding authored_sha256
mutations.why: Entry sha256 is validated as lowercase hex (HEX64_RE), so an authored_sha256 written in uppercase by a harness no longer matches after this mutant and the author-minted refusal silently misses. It also changes Manifest.core(), hence the manifest digest and manifest_digest in the core. Mirrors the Python from_dict lowercasing, which is equally unmutated.

mutations.name: manifest core() emits authored_sha256 unsorted
mutations.why: Python's core() emits sorted(self.authored_sha256). Dropping the sort makes the JS manifest digest depend on the order the harness happened to write the list in, so intact() fails and every rN span becomes UNRESOLVED manifest_integrity for any manifest whose list is not already sorted. The JCS region was mutated for key sorting but never for this domain-level sort.

mutations.name: SnapshotTree treats a symlink as a blob
mutations.why: GitTree explicitly refuses mode 120000 and the SnapshotTree docstring says it reproduces that rule. This mutant resolves a symlink's target-path bytes as if they were the committed file's contents — a path: receipt then swears against a filename string, and prereg: content-addressing can match a symlink blob. Whole tree layer is unmutated in the study.

mutations.name: canonical end offset read at the closer's far edge
mutations.why: CONTROL. Looks lethal — it changes which cut edge every span's end offset is read from — but both edges of a cut map to the same canonical offset by construction (boundaries[a] = a - removed_before, and boundaries[b] = b - removed_after = a - removed_before), including when an adjacent tag overwrites the entry. Verdicts, offsets and canonical_sha256 are all unchanged. It exists to measure whether the harness is detecting a real defect or merely noticing that a line moved.

mutations.name: render sorts its events, losing closer-before-opener adjacency
mutations.why: At an offset two spans share, sorting orders the tuples by tag bytes, putting b'</sworn>' before b'<sworn r=...>'; applied in reverse that emits the opener before the closer and reproduces `<sworn ...></sworn>` where the document had `</sworn><sworn ...>`. to_sidecar's asserted round trip then REFUSES a document it should have canonicalised, and verify()'s sidecar re-scan stops reproducing the span table. Nothing in the study mutates the sidecar layer.

mutations.name: load_sidecar admits a zero-length span
mutations.new: or not isinstance(b, int) or not (0 <= a <= b <= len(text))):
mutations.old: or not isinstance(b, int) or not (0 <= a < b <= len(text))):
mutations.why: The lexical_malformed_refuses_sidecar decision says a zero-byte span has no representable offsets: start == end cannot be ordered against a neighbour. This mutant lets one load, and render then produces `<sworn r=... k=...></sworn>`, which the lexer reads back as MALFORMED empty_span — so a sidecar that must be refused on load instead becomes a SWORN-FAILED document, and with two spans sharing an offset the re-scan ordering becomes ambiguous.

mutations.name: verify falls back to the tree handle's own commit
mutations.why: The rule is that receipts resolve at the commit the DOCUMENT names, and a document naming none gets no commit however the handle was built. This mutant lets a sidecar with commit null resolve path:/prereg: receipts against whatever commit the caller's GitTree was constructed with — the verdict becomes a function of the checkout, not of the bytes, and UNRESOLVED no_commit turns into HELD. The whole verify() reconciliation block is unmutated.

mutations.name: the receipt digest covers coverage again (R9 undone)
mutations.why: R9 exists so a receipt re-derives wherever the observer differs. With coverage back inside the digest body, issue_receipt still self-checks but verify_receipt's cmp_core keeps coverage while cmp_fresh drops it, so verdict_reproduces goes False for every /v1 receipt, and any observer difference (claimdetect absent, a different STRUCT1_VERSION) breaks the digest of a receipt whose verdict is byte-identical. One tuple decides this and nothing mutates it.

mutations.name: occurrences counts overlapping matches
mutations.why: countBytes carries a deliberate two-line construction so its result matches Python's non-overlapping bytes.count; this mutant leaves the superseding line as an advance-by-one and makes the count overlapping. `occurrences` is a detail field inside the digested core, so a self-overlapping quote needle produces a different core digest on the two implementations while every verdict string stays identical — precisely the class of divergence the 1689-vector agreement is supposed to catch.

produced: eight independent readers of styxx/sworn.py and styxx/_data/sworn_verify.js, one per region, each told to include mutations it suspected the generator could not reach; then a completeness critic that read both files and named what nobody had covered. No reader saw the harness's coverage, and none ran it (M2).
